b: Figure 5. Miliary TB: widespread, bilateral, fine reticulonodular opacities due to haematogenous dissemination. The tiny nodules may resemble millet seeds. Source: Herreros B, Plaza I, García R, Chichón M, Guerrero C and Pintor E, 2018, Pat

Clinical significance: Miliary TB is disseminated disease and may involve the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow and central nervous system. It is particularly important to recognise in young children and immunocompromised patients.

qs.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a 4-week history of remittent fever, night sweats, failure to thrive, and hepatosplenomegaly. Chest radiography reveals fine, uniform, widespread punctate nodularities. Which of the following findings is least characteristic of miliary tuberculosis?
qs.e: Sharp localized pleuritic chest pain is characteristic of localized pleural tuberculosis rather than disseminated miliary disease. Miliary tuberculosis is a hematogenous infection characterized by widespread systemic organ involvement and non-localized signs.
qs.s: Tuberculosis: Comprehensive Clinical & Pharmacology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with miliary tuberculosis undergoes a fundoscopic examination by an ophthalmologist. Which of the following specific findings might be visualized?
qs.e: Fundoscopy in miliary TB may show choroidal tubercles as a manifestation of blood-borne dissemination. Miliary TB itself presents with 2-3 weeks of fever, night sweats, and fine 1-2 mm lung lesions.

qs.q: Which of the following describes the radiographic appearance classically associated with miliary tuberculosis on a chest X-ray?
o: Unilateral pleural effusion with full opacification
Fine 1-2 mm lesions distributed across the lungs
A single massive cavitary lesion in the right lobe
qs.e: The classical appearances on chest X-ray for miliary TB are fine 1-2 mm lesions ('millet seed') distributed throughout the lung fields. Blood-borne dissemination gives rise to this presentation, sometimes accompanied by hepatosplenomegaly.
